questions.explanation: #1 closes the bounty and initiative 'effective today' but says responsible disclosure remains open, Least Authority continues as Ecosystem Security Lead, and reports submitted earlier are handled under the terms at the time. The tempting misreading is that closure means abandoning security or earlier submissions; #1 says neither, and its stated reason is report volume and triage load, not a shortage of valid reports.
options: It ends all security work and tells researchers to stop reporting, because AI tools have made human vulnerability research pointless to fund.
It closes the bounty and initiative but keeps private reporting open, keeps funding Least Authority's audit work, and says good-faith reports remain welcome.
It replaces the open bounty with a smaller tiered scheme, and cancels rewards for reports that were already submitted before the announcement.
It closes the bounty because the valid reports it received were too few to justify the cost, and hands vulnerability intake over to Zellic.
questions.prompt: Which description of the stance taken in the announcement (#1) is accurate rather than a caricature?

questions.explanation: #31 answers #3 by saying platforms face the same problems, citing a critical HackerOne report left untriaged for over three weeks. #32 replied that Immunefi and HackerOne are usually responsive for critical bugs, so the claim stayed contested. The other options are not objections anyone made: the severity point and the dev-team point appear in #32 as part of the proposal, not as arguments against it.
options: Outside platforms would take control of Zcash's disclosure process, which a decentralized project should not hand to commercial companies.
Platforms are slow on low-severity bugs but reliable on critical ones, so only critical reports should be moved to them.
A platform would not remove the triage problem: a critical report submitted to HackerOne had gone untriaged for more than three weeks.
The dev team should not set its mission aside to handle spam, so any platform triage would still have to be done in-house.
questions.prompt: One proposal was to move the bounty to platforms such as HackerOne, Immunefi or HackenProof. What was the main objection raised in the thread?

questions.explanation: The incentive argument in #3 and #32 was never answered by a later post. The platform proposal was contested by #31, the case for closing was contested by #3, #18, #32 and #37, and the omitted GHSA was confirmed by the Foundation in #67 after #61 raised it.
options: Without rewards, researchers' incentives would shift toward exploiting or reselling vulnerabilities, or toward rival bounty programs.
Moving the program to established platforms such as HackerOne or Immunefi would solve the triage problem for the program.
Closing the bounty program is the right response to the volume of duplicate and speculative vulnerability reports it received.
Zebra advisory GHSA-pvmv-cwg8-v6c8 was left out of the report that went to ZCG, so the payout for it was missed.
questions.prompt: Which of these arguments drew no direct reply from anyone in the thread?

questions.explanation: #67 says 'We did incorrectly miss out GHSA-pvmv-cwg8-v6c8 from our report sent to ZCG' and that it is following up to recommend payout, after #61 and #62 raised the missing payout. It does not concede the duplicate rule: it still says sangsoo's earlier report is the eligible one and fivelittleducks' was a duplicate.
options: That the report from fivelittleducks, rather than the earlier one, was the one the team acted on and is therefore eligible for the bounty.
That the duplicate rule is unfair to independent finders, so both reporters of the same issue should be paid the full reward.
That the v4.4.1 release notes had left one of the two reporters out of the credits, which should be corrected in the notes.
That the GHSA had been wrongly left out of the report sent to ZCG, and that a payout recommendation would now follow.
questions.prompt: In #67 a concession was made in response to payout questions about GHSA-pvmv-cwg8-v6c8. What was conceded?

questions.explanation: #69 rests on the quality and independence of the report (acknowledged in the advisory and v4.4.1 notes) and a public timeline of PR #10510, the May 3 submission, and PR #10542. It does not cite terms that split rewards; #67 states the opposite rule, that the disclosure which started remediation gets the reward.
options: The program's published terms, which split the reward whenever two researchers independently report the same Critical issue.
An earlier statement that severity assessments by the engineering teams were never meant to decide payout categories.
An independent, reproducible Critical report credited in the advisory, plus a public PR and release timeline showing v4.4.0 lacked the guard.
Agreement from the other reporter that both submissions were correct and that both of them deserved to be paid.
questions.prompt: In #69, what is offered as support for a partial or discretionary payout to a reporter whose submission was classified as a duplicate?

questions.explanation: #18 gives the fullest case: it concedes the program was unsustainable as designed, locates the flaw in the design, proposes concrete fixes, and says the original reason for opening still stands; #3 and #37 add that unrewarded disclosure is not enough. The goodwill option reverses #3, which says relying on goodwill is not enough.
options: Zcash is already audited by Least Authority, so a bounty adds little to security and should be kept only as a symbolic gesture to researchers.
The flaw was the design, not the idea: strict rules, clear PoC requirements and automated triage cut noise, and the risk of undiscovered 0-days still stands.
Researchers' goodwill toward the project is enough to keep disclosures coming, so a bounty can be reduced to a simple public thank-you list.
AI-assisted reports are mostly low quality, so a bounty should be restricted to accept only vulnerabilities that were found by hand.
questions.prompt: Which is the strongest case actually made in the thread for keeping a bounty in some form instead of closing it?

questions.explanation: #48 combines the duplicate burden, the cost of attributing first discovery, the risk to NU7 plans and the point that AI tools are open to everyone; #1 and #17 add that every report needs human triage and that the program cannot continue as is. The goodwill option misreads #1, which says it cannot incentivize the disclosure lottery, not that incentives do not matter.
options: Reports were largely duplicates of known issues, attributing first discovery would eat time and stall NU7 plans, and AI tools open to everyone found most bugs.
Closing costs nothing, since researchers report out of goodwill anyway and private reporting remains open for anyone who finds a vulnerability.
Bounties attract mainly dishonest researchers, so removing the payment filters out bad-faith reporters and leaves only genuine reports behind.
The reward budget was exhausted because the number of valid reports exceeded the program's cap, leaving nothing to pay out to later reporters.
questions.prompt: Which is the strongest case actually made in the thread for closing the bounty rather than redesigning it?

questions.explanation: #22 says ZODL has not brushed off reporters, its assessments are mainly for its own prioritization, and ZCG made the payout categories without its input; #23 says ZODL does not submit payout requests; #70 says he had no input into the program either. The payout-request part of the first option is the statement that #23 says is inaccurate.
options: ZODL assigned impact levels so ZCG could use them as payout tiers, and then filed payout requests for researchers after remediation.
ZODL set most reports aside because the volume was too high, which is why researchers were left unpaid and without answers.
The engineering teams co-designed the payout categories with ZCG, so their impact levels were meant to map directly onto those categories.
Their assessments served their own mitigation priorities, not ZCG's categories, which they did not help set; they report fixes to ZCG but file no payout requests.
questions.prompt: Which description of the engineering teams' stated role matches what daira and zancas say in #22, #23 and #70?
